prompt: Which graph is best for showing the temperature outside every hour during a school day?

feedback.b: Bar graphs suit data sorted into groups. This data changes over time.
feedback.c: Dot plots show how often each value happens, not how something changes over time.

hints: The temperature is measured again and again over time.
solution: The temperature is measured over time, so it is time-series data. A **time-series graph** shows how it changes.

prompt: On a time-series graph, what goes along the x-axis (across the bottom)?

feedback.b: The values go up the y-axis (the side).
feedback.c: The title goes at the top of the graph.
feedback.d: Categories go along the bottom of a bar graph, not a time-series graph.

hints: Think about what "time-series" means.
solution: On a time-series graph, **time** goes along the x-axis, in order from earliest to latest.

hints: An "upward …" or a "downward …".
solution: It is called a **trend**.

prompt: Select **all** the things a good graph should have.

options.text: A scale that starts at 0 with equal steps
Units, such as cm or °C, where needed

hints: Which things help someone read the graph correctly?
solution: A good graph needs **a title, axis labels, a scale from 0 with equal steps, and units**. Colours and 3D effects don’t make it easier to read.

prompt: Tama drew a time-series graph of the temperature. Along the x-axis he wrote the times 9 am, 11 am, 10 am, 12 pm. What is wrong?

options.text: The times must be in order, from earliest to latest.
Time should go up the y-axis instead.
He should have used a bar graph.

feedback.b: On a time-series graph, time goes along the x-axis.
feedback.c: Temperature over time is time-series data, so a time-series graph is right.
feedback.d: 11 am comes after 10 am, so the order is wrong.

hints: Read the times from left to right.
solution: Time must go in order along the x-axis: **9 am, 10 am, 11 am, 12 pm**. Otherwise the graph shows the changes in the wrong order.

prompt: On a time-series graph, [[a]] goes along the x-axis, and the points are joined with [[b]].
hints: Picture a graph of a sunflower's height measured every week. What goes along the bottom, and how are the dots connected?
solution: **Time** goes along the x-axis, and the points are joined with **straight lines**.

prompt: Put these steps for drawing a time-series graph in order.

items.text: Draw the x-axis and the y-axis.
Write the times along the x-axis, in order.
Choose a scale for the y-axis that starts at 0 and goes up in equal steps.
Plot a point for each time.
Join the points with straight lines.
Add a title and label both axes.

hints: You need the axes and scales before you can plot points.
solution: Draw the axes, put the times along the x-axis, choose a y-axis scale from 0, plot the points, join them with straight lines, and finally add a title and labels.

prompt: Which of these is time-series data?

options.text: The height of a seedling, measured every day for two weeks
The shoe size of everyone in Room 8
The number of pets each student has

feedback.b: This is category data: each student picks a colour. It isn’t collected over time.
feedback.c: Each person has one shoe size. It isn’t collected over time.
feedback.d: This is number data for different students, not one thing measured over time.

hints: Time-series data measures the same thing again and again over time.
solution: **The height of a seedling, measured every day** is time-series data: each height goes with a day.

prompt: A TV news graph shows how many people went to a summer festival: 900 last year and 1000 this year. The y-axis starts at 800, so this year’s bar looks twice as tall as last year’s. Explain why this graph could give people the wrong idea.
modelAnswer: The y-axis starts at 800 instead of 0, so the bars only show the part above 800 (100 and 200). That makes this year’s bar look twice as tall. But the crowd only went up by 100 people, from 900 to 1000, which is not double. Starting the scale at 0 would show that the bars are nearly the same height.

rubric.criterion: Says the scale does not start at 0, which makes the difference look bigger
Says the real increase is only 100 people (900 to 1000), which is nowhere near double

hints: What number should a bar graph’s scale start at?
Did the number of people really double?
solution: The scale starts at 800, not 0, so a small change looks huge. The crowd only grew by 100 (from 900 to 1000), not twice as many.
